","char_count":493,"fact_ids":[],"source_anchors":[]},{"section_id":"B","chunk_id":"sec03-B","merge_seq":2,"domain":null,"heading":"B — Dangerous driving","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## B — Audience and scope
The audience is an New Hampshire first-time passenger-car applicant studying dangerous driving. ","char_count":366,"fact_ids":[],"source_anchors":[]},{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"sec03-C","merge_seq":3,"domain":"Dangerous driving","heading":"C — Dangerous driving","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Licensing and examination knowledge
FACT_ID: sec03-F001 | anchor: P13
Poor vision may make traffic harder to recognize, hazards harder to notice and responses slower; the handbook recommends regular eye examinations.

FACT_ID: sec03-F002 | anchor: P13
A driver who needs corrective lenses must use them behind the wheel and should avoid dark or tinted corrective lenses at night.

FACT_ID: sec03-F003 | anchor: P13
Fatigue means extreme tiredness associated with causes such as exertion, illness, repetitive activity or inadequate sleep.

FACT_ID: sec03-F004 | anchor: P13
Tiredness can impair vision and delay driving decisions; avoid driving when fatigued.

FACT_ID: sec03-F005 | anchor: P13
The handbook compares the performance loss from extended wakefulness with alcohol-related impairment and places responsibility on the driver to avoid tired driving.

FACT_ID: sec03-F006 | anchor: P13
For ordinary daytime alertness, the manual recommends adequate sleep and gives an average range of seven through nine hours.

FACT_ID: sec03-F007 | anchor: P13
On a long journey, plan a break at least once every two hours to stretch or get a drink.

FACT_ID: sec03-F008 | anchor: P13
Before tiredness becomes severe, leave the road at an exit or rest area and take a 15-to-20-minute nap or find overnight accommodation.

FACT_ID: sec03-F009 | anchor: P13
Avoid late-night driving when possible and arrange for a companion to share the driving.

FACT_ID: sec03-F010 | anchor: P13
A distraction removes attention from driving; looking away, taking hands off the wheel and mentally disengaging can all increase crash risk.

FACT_ID: sec03-F011 | anchor: P13
The handheld-electronics prohibition covers a moving vehicle and brief traffic stops, including stops for traffic-control devices.

FACT_ID: sec03-F012 | anchor: P13
Prohibited handheld activities include electronic messaging, calls, internet requests, navigation-data entry and typing into portable electronic equipment.

FACT_ID: sec03-F013 | anchor: P14
Holding a voice-capable electronic device beside the ear while the vehicle moves creates a presumption that the driver is making a call.

FACT_ID: sec03-F014 | anchor: P14
Drivers under 18 cannot use either handheld or hands-free mobile electronics while driving or briefly stopped in traffic, except to report an emergency to emergency dispatch or a public-safety agency.

FACT_ID: sec03-F015 | anchor: P14
A permitted hands-free conversation uses equipment that allows conversation without holding the device; the definition permits a hand to activate, deactivate or start a function.

FACT_ID: sec03-F016 | anchor: P14
The manual's permitted hands-free use still requires that the driver keep attention on the road ahead.

FACT_ID: sec03-F017 | anchor: P14
The listed electronics exceptions include action required by an ignition-interlock device.

FACT_ID: sec03-F018 | anchor: P14
Avoid arguments and emotionally stressful conversations with passengers while driving.

FACT_ID: sec03-F019 | anchor: P14
Do not eat behind the wheel; secure children with appropriate restraints and carry pets in a secured carrier or portable kennel.

FACT_ID: sec03-F020 | anchor: P14
The operator remains responsible for attentive and safe operation despite the presence of passengers or devices.

FACT_ID: sec03-F021 | anchor: P14
Aggressive driving involves intentionally taking an action that places another person's safety or property at risk.

FACT_ID: sec03-F022 | anchor: P14
Aggressive behaviors include speeding, close following, unsafe lane changes, improper signals and disregarding traffic controls.

FACT_ID: sec03-F023 | anchor: P14
Concentrate on operating the vehicle and show patience and courtesy toward other road users.

FACT_ID: sec03-F024 | anchor: P14
For someone under 21, the manual prohibits control of a vehicle while impaired by alcohol, controlled drugs, prescriptions, nonprescription drugs or other impairing substances.

FACT_ID: sec03-F025 | anchor: P14
The stated alcohol-concentration threshold for an operator under 21 is zero point zero two percent or greater.

FACT_ID: sec03-F026 | anchor: P14
A driver under 21 may transport alcoholic beverages only while accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or spouse of legal age, under the stated exception.

FACT_ID: sec03-F027 | anchor: P14
Alcohol and other impairing substances can diminish judgment, vision and reaction speed.

FACT_ID: sec03-F028 | anchor: P15
Impaired judgment makes clear, quick driving decisions harder to perform.

FACT_ID: sec03-F029 | anchor: P15
Alcohol-related visual effects can include blur, double vision, slow focusing and poorer estimates of distance, speed or movement.

FACT_ID: sec03-F030 | anchor: P15
An impaired reaction slows the processing of information and the response to a driving task.

FACT_ID: sec03-F031 | anchor: P15
The handbook advises against driving any vehicle after consuming alcohol or impairing drugs and warns that even an initial drink can affect driving ability.

FACT_ID: sec03-F032 | anchor: P15
Prevent a friend or relative from driving after drinking or using an impairing drug.

FACT_ID: sec03-F033 | anchor: P15
Only time reduces alcohol's effects; coffee, meals, fresh air, exercise or cold showers may increase alertness without reversing impairment.

FACT_ID: sec03-F034 | anchor: P15
The handbook describes an initial impaired-driving conviction as a Class B misdemeanor with a fine of at least 500 dollars and possible privilege loss lasting nine months through two years.

Misconceptions: Treat closely related requirements as separate rules; preserve the triggering condition and any exception given in each fact [P13].
Mnemonics: Remember the condition together with the required action; this is an authored study cue.
Glossary: Definitions in the fact blocks keep the source context rather than substituting a broader rule.
Dynamic isolation: Source thresholds remain snapshot-specific until current official reconciliation.

FACT_ID: sec03-F035 | anchor: P15
Restoration after the described initial impaired-driving offense requires attendance at an approved impaired-driver education course.

FACT_ID: sec03-F036 | anchor: P15
Repeat impaired-driving convictions carry stronger penalties, including larger fines and longer suspensions.

FACT_ID: sec03-F037 | anchor: P15
Nonprescription remedies for pain, colds, allergies or nervousness can cause drowsiness and affect driving.

FACT_ID: sec03-F038 | anchor: P15
Stimulant or diet pills can produce nervousness, dizziness, concentration problems or visual effects that interfere with driving.

FACT_ID: sec03-F039 | anchor: P15
Read a medicine's warnings before use, and ask a doctor or pharmacist about driving effects when uncertain.

FACT_ID: sec03-F040 | anchor: P15
Prescription medicines can impair reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness; the examples include antidepressants, pain medicines, sleep aids and sedatives.

FACT_ID: sec03-F041 | anchor: P15
Illegal drugs can impair driving functions, and driving under their influence is unlawful and dangerous.

FACT_ID: sec03-F042 | anchor: P15
Avoid alcohol while taking other drugs because their effects can combine with or amplify alcohol-related impairment.

FACT_ID: sec03-F043 | anchor: P15
Strong emotions, including worry, excitement, fear, anger or depression, can interfere with information processing and safe driving.

FACT_ID: sec03-F044 | anchor: P16
Calm down before driving; the handbook suggests a short walk or nap as possible ways to settle strong emotions.

FACT_ID: sec03-F045 | anchor: P16
Allow extra departure time and plan for traffic or poor weather to reduce stressful driving situations.

FACT_ID: sec03-F046 | anchor: P16
Let another person drive when emotions interfere with safe operation.

FACT_ID: sec03-F047 | anchor: P16
A parked vehicle starts heating immediately in warm weather and can become dangerously hot within minutes.

FACT_ID: sec03-F048 | anchor: P16
Do not leave a child alone in a vehicle for any duration.

FACT_ID: sec03-F049 | anchor: P16
Check the entire vehicle, with particular attention to the rear seat, before locking it and walking away.

FACT_ID: sec03-F050 | anchor: P16
Putting a personal item in the rear seat can serve as a reminder to inspect that seat before leaving the vehicle.

FACT_ID: sec03-F051 | anchor: P16
Keep keys and key fobs beyond children's reach and teach children that vehicles are not places to play.

Handoff hints: Group the cited facts by their actual subject and condition. Use prerequisite relations only where one stated definition is needed to understand another fact. Pedagogic emphasis is authored, because official test-domain weighting is unavailable. Confusable rules retain all different qualifiers and source pages.
